media:group.media:title: Penn vs Cornell, Thanksgiving Day 1915
media:group.media:description: The oldest film in Penn’s University Archives & Records Center documents the 1915 football game featuring Penn versus Cornell, played on Thanksgiving Day in front of a packed crowd at Franklin Field. Produced by the Alumni Society, the black-and-white silent film features football players scrambling on the field, cheerleaders performing, a band playing, and fans celebrating, spilling out of the bleachers.

entry.title: Penn women talk leadership, mentorship, and trailblazing

media:group.media:title: Penn women talk leadership, mentorship, and trailblazing
media:group.media:description:
The 2026 Silfen Forum explored the theme of ‘150 Years of Penn Women: Progress and the Path Forward’ with five barrier-breaking Penn women.
The panel for this year’s Silfen Forum, which became a Penn tradition in 2009, included Ambassador Amy Gutmann, who served as Penn President from 2004-2022; Virginia M.-Y. Lee, the John H. Ware 3rd Endowed Professor in Alzheimer’s Research at the Perelman School of Medicine; Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle L. Parker, a Fels Institute of Government alumna and the City’s first female and Black female mayor; and Penn President Emerita—and first permanent female Penn president—Judith Rodin. Moderating the panel was NBC News’ Chief Washington Correspondent and Chief Foreign Affairs Andrea Mitchell, a Penn alumna and trustee emerita.
To learn more about the Silfen Forum and view past events, visit https://silfenforum.upenn.edu/
#UPenn #WomensHistory #SilfenForum

entry.title: Celebrating 150 Years of Women at Penn

media:group.media:title: Celebrating 150 Years of Women at Penn
media:group.media:description:
Every day at Penn, women are discovering, creating, healing, teaching, competing and innovating. It wasn’t always this way. In 1876, the first women students arrived on campus, and they changed the University of Pennsylvania for good.
This year Penn marks 150 years since women first enrolled. Gertrude K. Peirce and Anna Lockhart Flanigen came to study the sciences, with the support of chemistry professor and future Provost Edgar Fahs Smith. Women were first admitted as “special students” in graduate study and earned certificates, not degrees. Only in the 20th century did they gradually gain entry to undergraduate degree programs. Again and again, the breakthroughs came from groups of women working together.
📍 See the exhibit: “150 Years of Women at Penn” is on view at Penn Libraries, first floor of the Van Pelt-Dietrich Library Center, through Dec. 11. Free and open to the public.
🔗 Explore the anniversary: https://www.upenn.edu/about/history/150-years-women-at-penn 📰 Read the story on Penn Today: https://penntoday.upenn.edu/news/150-years-women-penn
#UPenn #WomensHistory

entry.title: Penn professor Emily Wilson reads from her translation of Homer’s “The Iliad”

media:group.media:title: Penn professor Emily Wilson reads from her translation of Homer’s “The Iliad”
media:group.media:description: Emily Wilson, professor of classical studies at Penn, has become renowned for her translations of Homer’s epic poems, “The Iliad,” published in September, and “The Odyssey,” published in 2017. Standing center stage, Emily is in the spotlight, reading aloud lines from “The Iliad,” first in the original Greek, and then in her English translation.
